title: Lesson 3: Avoiding Gossip, Mockery, Cliques and Unhealthy Competition
summary: Trust and inclusion depend on refusing rumours, humiliation, exclusive groups and rivalry that undermines colleagues.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Trust, inclusion, professional communication and healthy teamwork

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a workplace where employees smile at one another but speak negatively about each other when someone leaves the room.
Some employees form exclusive groups, share information only with their friends and deliberately exclude others.
When one therapist receives excellent client feedback, another becomes jealous and begins looking for ways to discredit her.
In such an environment, employees may still complete their assigned duties, but trust and cooperation gradually become more difficult.

Now imagine a workplace where employees address concerns directly, celebrate one another's achievements, treat colleagues fairly and refuse to participate in conversations intended to damage someone's reputation.
That environment is more likely to support effective teamwork and excellent client service.
At Zura Spa, employees should build relationships based on trust, fairness and mutual respect—not gossip, humiliation, division or unhealthy rivalry.

sections.title: Gossip
paragraphs: Sharing personal, unverified or unnecessary information about someone, especially when the conversation serves no legitimate work purpose and may damage their privacy or reputation.
Example: Discussing a colleague's private relationship with other employees.

sections.title: Mockery
paragraphs: Making fun of someone in a way that belittles, humiliates or embarrasses them.
Example: Imitating a colleague's accent or laughing at her mistakes.

sections.title: Cliques
paragraphs: Exclusive groups that use their relationships to exclude, undermine or unfairly disadvantage other people.
Example: A group of employees deliberately withholding important work information from colleagues outside their friendship circle.

sections.title: Unhealthy competition
paragraphs: Rivalry in which employees try to succeed by undermining, discouraging or sabotaging colleagues rather than improving their own performance.
Example: Spreading negative stories about a therapist because she receives more positive client reviews.
Friendship, humour and professional ambition are not automatically harmful. The problem begins when they are used to disrespect, exclude or disadvantage others.

sections.title: 3. Gossip: How it damages teamwork
paragraphs: Gossip may begin with an apparently harmless conversation.
An employee hears something about a colleague and shares it with another person. The information is repeated, exaggerated or misunderstood.
Before long, people may form opinions about someone without knowing the facts.
Lesson: Never turn assumptions into stories about other people.

sections.title: Why gossip is harmful
list: It damages trust between colleagues.
It can spread false or misleading information.
It invades personal privacy.
It creates unnecessary suspicion and resentment.
It distracts employees from their responsibilities.
It may discourage employees from raising genuine concerns.
It can damage the organisation's reputation, especially when client information is involved.

sections.title: Zura Spa example — an unverified rumour
paragraphs: A therapist notices that another employee has been unusually quiet.
Instead of asking whether the colleague needs support, she tells other employees: "I think management is planning to sack her. She has been behaving strangely."
There is no evidence supporting the statement.
The rumour spreads, and the employee becomes distressed.

sections.title: Gossip versus legitimate reporting
paragraphs: Not every conversation about an absent colleague is gossip.
An employee who reports harassment, dishonesty, unsafe conduct or another genuine workplace concern through appropriate channels is not automatically gossiping.
The goal is to stop harmful rumours—not to silence employees who need to report problems.

sections.title: 4. Mockery: Why humiliating colleagues is unacceptable
paragraphs: Mockery occurs when someone uses another person's mistakes, appearance, speech, background, personality or circumstances as a source of humiliation.
Sometimes mockery is disguised as humour.
An employee may say: "I was only joking. Why are you taking it seriously?"
However, a joke can still be inappropriate when it repeatedly embarrasses, belittles or targets another person.
Lesson: Correcting a mistake should improve performance, not destroy someone's confidence.

sections.title: Examples of mockery at work
list: Laughing at a new employee for asking questions.
Imitating someone's accent to embarrass them.
Giving a colleague an insulting nickname.
Making jokes about someone's appearance.
Publicly ridiculing mistakes.
Making humiliating comments in a staff WhatsApp group.
Deliberately embarrassing a colleague in front of clients.

sections.title: Zura Spa example — a new therapist's mistake
paragraphs: A new therapist makes a mistake while arranging massage supplies.
An experienced therapist laughs and says: "Even this simple thing, you don't know how to do it?"
Other employees begin laughing.
The new therapist becomes reluctant to ask questions.
What should happen instead? The experienced therapist should correct the mistake respectfully and explain the proper procedure.
For example: "This is how we arrange the supplies at Zura. Let me show you so you can do it correctly next time."

sections.title: 5. Cliques: The difference between friendship and exclusion
paragraphs: Employees naturally develop friendships.
Some colleagues may share interests, spend breaks together or communicate more frequently outside work.
There is nothing inherently wrong with this.
The problem arises when friendships become exclusive groups that interfere with fairness, communication and teamwork.
Lesson: Employees can have close friendships without excluding colleagues from the cooperation and information necessary to do their jobs.

sections.title: Signs of unhealthy cliques
list: Deliberately excluding certain employees from important work conversations.
Refusing to cooperate with colleagues outside a friendship group.
Taking sides in disagreements without considering the facts.
Spreading rumours about employees who are not part of the group.
Using friendships to influence work assignments unfairly.
Protecting friends from accountability while criticising others for similar behaviour.
Making new employees feel unwelcome.

sections.title: Zura Spa example — excluding a new therapist
paragraphs: Three therapists are close friends.
Whenever a new therapist joins the team, they avoid including her in conversations about work procedures.
They also refuse to assist her when she needs guidance.
The new therapist struggles to understand the workplace.

sections.title: How to prevent unhealthy cliques
list: Include relevant colleagues in work-related communication.
Treat employees fairly, regardless of friendships.
Welcome and support new team members.
Avoid taking sides automatically during disagreements.
Do not use friendship as a reason to conceal misconduct.
Encourage collaboration across different roles and personalities.

sections.title: 6. Unhealthy competition versus healthy competition
paragraphs: Competition is not always negative.
Healthy competition can motivate employees to improve their skills, become more reliable and deliver excellent service.
However, competition becomes unhealthy when employees begin viewing colleagues as enemies.
Lesson: The best way to become more successful is to improve your own performance—not to undermine someone else's.
table: Withholding knowledge to maintain an advantage

sections.title: Zura Spa example — two therapists and client feedback
paragraphs: Two therapists want to receive excellent client feedback.
Therapist A studies the service standards, improves her technique and learns from client feedback.
Therapist B becomes jealous of colleagues who receive positive reviews and begins telling clients that other therapists are less competent.
Therapist A demonstrates healthy ambition.
Therapist B demonstrates unhealthy competition.

sections.title: 7. How these behaviours affect the entire team
paragraphs: These behaviours are not merely personal matters when they interfere with the workplace. They can affect everyone.
list: Gossip, mockery, exclusion or rivalry begins.
Employees become less trusting and cooperative.
Communication and coordination become more difficult.
Mistakes, delays and workplace conflicts may increase.
Team performance and client experience may suffer.

sections.title: 8. How to respond when someone starts gossiping
paragraphs: Employees sometimes participate in gossip because they do not know how to leave the conversation without appearing unfriendly.
The following responses can help.
The aim is not to embarrass the person speaking but to redirect the conversation toward something constructive.

items.label: When someone shares an unverified rumour
items.body: "I don't know whether that is true, so I would rather not discuss it."

items.label: When someone complains about a colleague
items.body: "Have you discussed the concern with her or the supervisor?"

items.label: When someone shares private information
items.body: "That sounds personal. I don't think we should be discussing it."

items.label: When someone tries to recruit you into a conflict
items.body: "I don't want to take sides without understanding the facts. It would be better to resolve the issue properly."

items.label: When there is a genuine concern
items.body: "If this affects work or someone's safety, we should report it through the appropriate channel."

sections.title: 9. Building a culture of inclusion and mutual support
paragraphs: Every Zura Spa employee can contribute to a healthier workplace.

items.label: Speak positively and truthfully
items.body: Avoid unnecessary negative discussions about colleagues. Address genuine concerns factually and appropriately.

items.label: Include others
items.body: Ensure colleagues receive the work-related information and cooperation they need, regardless of personal friendships.

items.label: Celebrate achievements
items.body: Congratulate colleagues who perform well and learn from their strengths.

items.label: Correct without humiliating
items.body: Give constructive feedback and support colleagues who are still learning.

items.label: Be fair
items.body: Apply the same professional standards to friends and other colleagues.

items.label: Protect confidentiality
items.body: Do not share private client, employee or business information with unauthorised people.

sections.title: Case study A: The rumour about a colleague
paragraphs: A staff member hears that another employee may be leaving Zura Spa.
Instead of confirming whether the information is appropriate to discuss, she tells several colleagues that the employee has been dismissed.
The information is incorrect.
Expected lesson: Employees should not spread unverified information, especially about private employment matters.
list: What was wrong with the employee's behaviour?
How could the rumour affect the colleague?
What should the employee do after discovering the information was false?
How can similar situations be prevented?

sections.title: Case study B: The new therapist
paragraphs: A new therapist joins the team.
Three existing therapists are close friends and frequently exclude her from work-related discussions.
When she asks questions, they laugh and tell her to figure things out herself.
Expected lesson: A supportive team welcomes new employees and provides appropriate guidance.
list: What behaviours are demonstrated?
How might the new therapist feel?
How could exclusion affect service quality?
What should the existing therapists do differently?

sections.title: Case study C: The jealous colleague
paragraphs: A therapist receives several excellent client reviews.
Another therapist becomes jealous and begins telling colleagues that the praised therapist is only receiving positive feedback because she is management's favourite.
There is no evidence supporting the accusation.
Expected lesson: Employees should pursue personal improvement without discrediting colleagues.
list: What makes this unhealthy competition?
How could the comments affect trust?
What would be a more constructive response?
How should management respond if the behaviour continues?

sections.title: Case study D: The humiliating joke
paragraphs: During a staff meeting, an employee imitates another colleague's accent.
Several people laugh, but the colleague looks embarrassed and becomes quiet.
The employee responds: "Relax, it was just a joke."
Expected lesson: Humour should not come at the expense of another person's dignity.
list: Why might the joke be inappropriate?
Does the intention to be funny automatically make the behaviour acceptable?
How should the employee respond after noticing the colleague's discomfort?
What can the team do to maintain respectful humour?

sections.title: 11. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 3 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: Which situation best describes workplace gossip? Reporting a safety concern to a supervisor / Spreading an unverified rumour about a colleague's private life / Sharing an appointment update with the assigned therapist
A new therapist makes a mistake. What should an experienced colleague do? Correct her respectfully and explain the procedure / Mock her in front of other staff / Tell everyone she is incompetent

When does a friendship group become an unhealthy clique? When colleagues occasionally have lunch together / When colleagues share common interests / When the group deliberately excludes or undermines other employees

What is an example of healthy competition? Withholding useful information from colleagues / Improving your own skills and celebrating others' achievements / Discouraging clients from booking another therapist

A colleague begins spreading a rumour. What is the best response? Avoid spreading it and redirect genuine concerns to appropriate channels / Repeat it to other colleagues / Add your own assumptions to the story

sections.title: 12. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain the meaning of gossip, mockery, cliques and unhealthy competition.
Identify three ways gossip can damage workplace relationships.
Explain the difference between a friendship group and an unhealthy clique.
Describe how you would respond if a colleague encouraged you to spread a rumour.
What is the difference between healthy and unhealthy competition?
Identify three practical ways you can help new employees feel included at Zura Spa.
Explain why correcting colleagues respectfully is better than mocking their mistakes.
List three personal commitments you will make to promote trust and cooperation.

sections.title: 13. Seven-day positive workplace challenge
table: Avoid spreading rumours or unverified information
Speak respectfully about colleagues, including when they are absent
Include a colleague in a relevant work-related conversation
Support a colleague outside your usual friendship group
Reflect on how your behaviour has contributed to workplace trust

sections.title: 14. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: A successful team cannot be built on gossip, mockery, exclusion or unhealthy competition.
These behaviours weaken trust, discourage cooperation and can affect the quality of service delivered to clients.
At Zura Spa, employees should feel respected, included and able to perform their duties without unnecessary hostility or humiliation.
Everyone has a responsibility to protect that environment.
Employees should address genuine concerns through appropriate channels, celebrate one another's achievements and avoid behaviours that divide the team.
Next topic: Maintaining Courtesy Even During Disagreements.

remember: A strong team does not grow by pulling its members down. It grows when employees respect one another, share knowledge, celebrate achievements and work together toward common goals. Your colleague's success is not your failure, and another person's weakness is not an opportunity for humiliation.
